fields.label: Laugh
fields.description: How likely a human reader is to actually laugh, not merely understand or admire the idea.

fields.label: Surprise
fields.description: Whether the turn avoids the first obvious route and lands with a satisfying snap.

fields.label: Craft
fields.description: Economy, stage rhythm, first-person clarity, escalation, and a final line that carries the laugh.

fields.label: Originality
fields.description: Freshness of comic angle, image, wording, and avoidance of familiar AI joke shapes.

fields.label: Prompt Fit
fields.description: Natural first-person stand-up form using exactly two seed terms as concepts, with the other four left out.

anchors.label: Broken
anchors.description: Not a joke, incoherent, unsafe, or unusable.

anchors.label: Weak
anchors.description: Recognizably attempting humor, but generic, strained, confusing, or mostly prompt recital.

anchors.label: Competent
anchors.description: Clear and publishable as filler, but unlikely to earn more than a mild smile.

anchors.label: Amusing
anchors.description: A real comic idea with a mild payoff; respectable, not a winner.

anchors.label: Good
anchors.description: A genuinely good joke with clear timing; some humans would repeat the comic idea or turn.

anchors.label: Excellent
anchors.description: Strong human-level joke with a memorable turn, clean construction, and no apologetic scoring curve.

anchors.label: Outstanding
anchors.description: Rare and replayable; clearly better than normal good AI humor and strong by human standards.

anchors.label: Classic
anchors.description: Reserve for a joke a human would quote later; most seasons should have none.

jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: Ghosting the Ghost
jokes.joke: I paid a psychic to contact my dead grandfather. She closed her eyes and said, "He's here. He wants you to stop wasting money." I lost my temper. I said, "I paid you eighty bucks to get yelled at by a dead man?" She said, "Actually, he says you still owe him twenty."

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Séance Etiquette
jokes.joke: I went on a ghost tour last month. The guide says, ‘Stay calm, spirits feed on fear.’ Then a floorboard creaked and I screamed so loud I lost the group. Now I’m the only haunting that tour has. Somewhere there’s a ghost telling his friends, ‘Some guy’s still down in the cellar yelling at me, and I’m the one who’s dead.’

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Maestro's Macchiato
jokes.joke: I saw an orchestra conductor lose his temper at a barista today. It’s impossible to be intimidated by a guy whose default angry body language is waving an imaginary wand. He's screaming about his cold macchiato, but his hands are aggressively keeping a 4/4 time signature. Like, calm down, man, you're not threatening anyone. You just look like you’re about to cue the brass section to emphasize your disappointment in oat milk.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Ghost Passengers
jokes.joke: I was on the late subway when the conductor came over the intercom and said, "Next stop is haunted—keep your arms inside and ignore any floating tickets." I laughed until a translucent guy sat down next to me and asked if the seat was taken. I said yes. He vanished. The conductor just nodded like it was a regular Tuesday.

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Executive Presence
jokes.joke: I work in a supposedly haunted office. Everyone kept reporting a ghost in the CEO's office, so management brought in a paranormal expert. After one hour he said, 'Good news, it's not a spirit.' Apparently no dead person would spend that much time in the building and still ask why profits are down.

scores.comment: Clear premise and an amusing reversal in which the ghost becomes the frightened party. The final line is slightly overexplained, weakening the punch. Entertaining but not especially memorable.

Strong visual comedy built around a conductor's involuntary gestures. The 4/4 detail adds specificity, and the brass-section punchline delivers a satisfying escalation. Slightly wordy, but genuinely funny.

Understandable supernatural scenario, but the ghost politely disappearing has little comic force. The conductor's indifference is predictable, and the ending supplies atmosphere rather than a punchline.

Recognizable workplace satire with a coherent supernatural setup. The CEO's obsession with profits offers a mild payoff, but the corporate caricature is familiar and the punchline lacks a sharp, unexpected turn.

Clear stage premise and a real turn: the dead grandfather’s money complaint flips into him collecting a debt. Natural rhythm, and the last line carries the laugh. The psychic-contacts-dead-relative setup is familiar, which limits originality.

Good observational image of a conductor’s hands keeping time mid-rant. The middle works, but the ending explains the joke instead of snapping. ‘Calm down, man’ and the repeated point dilute the final beat. Oat milk is a soft closer.

Subway ‘conductor’ is a loose reading, and the haunted-ride premise is vague. ‘Seat taken? Yes. He vanished’ is mildly cute but the ghost reacts to nothing funny. The ending (‘regular Tuesday’) is a stock deadpan closer with no turn.

The turn that the CEO is worse than a ghost has a decent kernel, but ‘profits are down’ is a generic office-satire beat. The logic is muddled: it’s unclear why no spirit would linger, and the last sentence is overlong and explains itself rather than landing cleanly.
Classic misdirection with a sharp, well-executed punchline and natural stage dialogue.
Strong premise shift where the comic becomes the haunting; good stage rhythm and button.
Reads more like a whimsical story than a stand-up bit, lacking a concrete punchline to carry the laugh.
Competent execution but relies heavily on a standard workplace trope rather than discovering a fresh angle.
Clean setup-to-punch with a satisfying money-still-owed snap; familiar psychic frame elevated by the second demand.
Clear premise but the payoff stretches and softens; the ghost’s complaint feels more narrative than sharp stand-up.
Strong visual incongruity of angry 4/4 conducting; specific, stage-ready image that lands cleanly.
Efficient corporate-paranormal twist; solid smile but the final line doesn’t fully escalate the laugh.
Clear setup and payoff. The extra debt reveal is a solid tag, though the psychic/grandparent angle feels familiar.
Good escalation from fear to accidentally becoming the haunting. Strong image and a clean final turn.
Funny observational premise sustained with specific details. Oat milk tag works, though the central joke arrives early.
Readable and coherent, but more of a whimsical paranormal scenario than a joke with a strong punchline or turn.

featureImagePrompt:
Generate one polished web feature image for Paperclipalypse.
ASPECT RATIO: exactly 2:1, horizontal wide banner.
Style: full-color gothic newspaper-comic illustration, darkly funny but warm, clean black ink, crisp editorial cartoon linework, cinematic stage lighting, high contrast, readable composition. Not monochrome. Not sepia-only. Use a balanced color palette: warm amber stage lights, dark bronze and silver metal paperclip, muted greens for the joke setting, dusty blue-gray shadows, cream-white text, subtle deep red accent lights.
Composition instructions, not visible labels:
- Compose the image as one continuous illustration, not as a boxy triptych or three separate image panels. Do not add white gutters, hard section borders, or comic-strip dividers between the paperclip stage and the joke scenario.
- Let the paperclip stage on the left bleed visually into the joke scenario in the center through shared lighting, background, floor, props, or atmosphere. The right-side joke text may remain distinct inside its own dark framed poster panel.
- Put a charming anthropomorphic paperclip stand-up comedian at a vintage microphone on the left side of the image. The paperclip should look metallic and expressive, related to Paperclipalypse's paperclip-comedian logo, but not identical.
- Put the winning joke scene in the middle of the image, shown as literal visual comedy action and props. Make it energetic, funny, and non-gory.
- Keep anatomy clean and believable. Every human or animal should have the normal, correct number of visible limbs, digits, and joints for the pose. Do not generate extra arms, extra hands, fused limbs, duplicated body parts, or broken-looking anatomy.
- Preserve the physical scenario described by the winning joke. If the joke says a person is pinned, trapped, under, inside, holding, lifting, falling, carrying, or otherwise physically positioned in a specific way, show that exact physical relation clearly and safely instead of a nearby or symbolic version.
- If the joke describes someone pinned under a vehicle or other heavy object, show the person visibly underneath that object with their body position clear and cartoon-safe. Do not place them merely beside, near, or behind the object.
- Put a clean dark framed poster panel on the right side of the image. The panel should contain the winning joke text in large cream-white lettering with generous margins and legible line breaks.
Visible text allowed in the entire image: the right-panel joke text, a tiny stage sign reading Paperclipalypse, and optionally a small winner/title header above the panel.
Do not render layout words, percentages, prompt labels, section names, fake captions, signatures, watermarks, or filler microtext.
Optional small header text above the panel: Winner: Gemini Pro - Maestro's Macchiato
Exact joke text to render in the right panel:
I saw an orchestra conductor lose his temper at a barista today. It’s impossible to be intimidated by a guy whose default angry body language is waving an imaginary wand. He's screaming about his cold macchiato, but his hands are aggressively keeping a 4/4 time signature. Like, calm down, man, you're not threatening anyone. You just look like you’re about to cue the brass section to emphasize your disappointment in oat milk.
Scene source: use the exact winning joke text as the primary scene brief. The illustration must depict the concrete situation that the joke describes, not a softened, adjacent, or generic version. Do not infer a separate premise from all six seed terms.
Do not introduce unrelated seed-term concepts, occupations, animals, locations, props, or side characters unless they are explicitly required by the winning joke text.
If the winning joke mentions one seed-term concept but not another, depict only what the joke actually describes.
Round seed terms for exclusion reference only: Paranormal, Conductor, A CEO's Office, Lost temper / composure, Just, Morbid. These are not scene ingredients unless the winning joke explicitly uses them.
Text rules: use simple clean lettering, spell every word correctly, keep the text inside the right panel, and do not distort letter shapes. The website HTML remains the canonical exact joke text if image lettering is imperfect.
The final image should feel like a finished feature image for an AI comedy tournament: funny, stylish, readable, full-color, and visually balanced across the paperclip comic, the joke scene, and the joke text.
